To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) learning a causal network is as hard as learning a distribution; (ii) the total variation distance is a good distance metric for causal networks; (iii) the squared Hellinger metric is not good for causal networks, and (iv) adaptivity does not always help in testing causal networks.

(1) non-adaptive interventions are sufficient to distinguish between unknown causal Bayesian networks with bounded in-degrees and bounded confounded components; and (2) adaptivity does not provide any advantage in this setting.

(1) the total variation distance between causal Bayesian networks is subadditive under interventions; and that (2) O(logn) interventions on an arbitrary graph with bounded in-degree and a constant number of confounded components suffice for testing the identity and learning a causal Bayesian net- work, and that adaptivity does no help in testing the identity of causal Bayesian networks.

the question of what can be learned about the causal structure of a system, given only a limited number of observations.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that the causal setting is much more powerful than the classical setting.
we provide the first sample efficient algorithms for testing and learning causal Bayesian networks.

we show how to efficiently solve the following three fundamental problems in causal inference: (i) distinguishing whether two causal models on the same graph are identical, (ii) distinguishing whether two interventions on the same causal model are equivalent, and (iii) learning an unknown causal model on a given graph, all in a nonadaptive fashion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for causal inference, the number of interventions required for testing or learning is independent of the size of the causal Bayesian network and depends only on the size of the underlying graph.
causal inference is not fundamentally different from statistical inference.
, in the causal setting, interventions can help in learning and testing problems in a way that is not possible in the standard non-interventionist setting.
